items.title: Lego stores opening soon at Square One in Mississauga and Eaton Centre Toronto
items.summary: Lego is expanding, with stores opening soon in Mississauga and Toronto. The company just opened a new location at CF Markville in Markham on Sept. 11, according to CF Markville. The approximately 2,690 square feet Lego Store is the first for the community, according to reports. And two more stores are scheduled to open at CF Toronto Eaton Centre and Square One Shopping Centre this fall. Both malls have the locations marked as “coming soon,” but Retail Insider is reporting the opening dates. The Eaton Centre location is scheduled to open on Oct. 23, and the Square One store will open on Nov. 6, according to Retail Insider. Lego did not immediately respond to a request for comment on when the new stores in the Greater Toronto Area will be opening. Signage went up on the storefronts a few months ago. The Eaton Centre store will be on Level 3, near the Queen Street entrance and next to Athleta.

items.title: Building of data centres paused for at least one year in Mississauga
items.summary: The building of large data centres in Mississauga has been halted for at least one year, city council decided on Wednesday morning. City of Mississauga councillors were unanimous in their support of an interim control bylaw that will impose a moratorium of one year — and up to two years — on data centre developments in Mississauga to allow the city more time to study the matter and any new rules that would regulate the rapidly growing industry. items.title: Courtneypark Athletic Fields will gain 1,175 native trees and shrubs
items.summary: On Sept. 19, volunteers, along with representatives from TD, will plant 525 native trees and shrubs at the site in a single morning. The event aims to move Mississauga closer to its goal of planting one million trees by 2032. Mississauga is planning to plant 1,175 native trees and shrubs at Courtneypark Athletic Fields over three dates in September and October to advance the city’s goal of planting one million trees by 2032. The tree planting series kicks off on Sept. 19, when volunteers and TD representatives will plant 525 native trees and shrubs in a single morning, one of the largest TD Tree Days events in Canada, the city said in a press release. The tree planting will continue on Oct. 3 and Oct. 17 at the same site located at 600 Courtneypark Dr. , bringing the total of planted trees and shrubs to 1,175 to naturalize nearly one hectare of previously mowed turf grass, a city spokesperson told the Mississauga News in an email. The city said that the site’s location, adjacent to Highway 401, makes it well-suited for vegetation that can help filter airborne pollutants and improve local air quality. The large-scale planting drive will provide a range of environmental benefits, including increased carbon sequestration, reduced urban heat island effects, improved stormwater infiltration and enhanced habitat for birds, pollinators and wildlife, the spokesperson said in the email. The project is also intended to strengthen connections within Mississauga’s broader natural heritage system, serving as an ecological stepping-stone in and beyond the Fletcher’s Creek watershed.

items.title: Mississauga council to consider backyard hen exemption for Ward 2 homeowner
items.summary: If approved, the exemption will only apply to one Ward 2 resident, who will be subject to the city animal care and control bylaw. Under existing city bylaws, all chickens, hens and pheasants are designated as prohibited species on private residential properties in Mississauga. At the Sept. 16 council meeting, Mississauga city councillors will consider a motion to grant a unique exemption to a Ward 2 resident who wants to keep urban hens and pheasants as pets. The motion by Coun. Alvin Tedjo proposes a unique exemption, allowing a Hartland Drive homeowner to keep the birds on his property for the duration of their lifespans. The resident came to Animal Services’ attention following a complaint about keeping prohibited species on residential property. However, the motion notes that immediate neighbours are aware of the pets and have no objections. In May 2021, Mississauga launched a two-year Urban Hen Pilot program to explore the feasibility of allowing residents to keep backyard chickens. The program permitted 11 households to participate across the city with a limit of four hens each to assess community interest and municipal impacts. However, council voted to end the program in November 2023 after staff recommended that chickens remain a prohibited species under city bylaws. The decision resulted from low uptake as only six households participated in the program, along with concerns of attracting wildlife such as coyotes, limited availability of veterinary support for poultry and risks of avian influenza, according to a city press release.

Condo developers have their sights set on the area surrounding the Port Credit GO station, where an underground stop for the new Hurontario LRT is under construction. Mississauga’s next city council could decide the fate of proposed zoning changes that would reshape how much housing and development can be built around 35 major transit station areas (MTSA). On June 10, Mississauga’s planning and development committee approved the proposed pre-zoning changes. However, the implementing zoning bylaw has yet to come before council for a final vote. That means the council elected this fall could ultimately decide whether the new rules actually come into effect. The issue is particularly relevant in Ward 1, where incumbent Coun. Stephen Dasko is in an election race against Olivia Gannon, and where Port Credit is already seeing significant development around its GO and future LRT stations. While there is broad consensus among the two Ward 1 candidates and community representatives that Mississauga needs increased housing closer to transit, concerns remain over how much density neighbourhoods should absorb and how much influence residents may have over individual projects.

items.title: Women in Mississauga, Brampton, Caledon face new digital threats as Take Back the Night returns
items.summary: Women have long been told to watch where they walk after dark, keep their earbuds out and stay alert to what is happening around them. But in 2026, the threats don’t necessarily stop when someone gets home. The internet, social media, online gaming and artificial intelligence have created new ways for sexual and gender-based violence to follow people wherever they go, according to one of the organizers of this week’s Take Back the Night event in Peel Region. The annual rally and march takes place Thursday, Sept. 17, at the TMU Integrated Health Centre at 74 Queen Street West in Brampton, bringing together survivors, advocates, allies and community organizations from across Brampton, Mississauga and Caledon. Rebecca Pacheco, coordinator of the Peel Committee Against Women Abuse (PCAWA) and director of professional practice and advocacy at Embrave Agency to End Violence, said the event is about much more than simply walking through the streets at night. “Take Back the Night is taking back a time that we’re continuously told is dangerous to us,” Pacheco said. Women are routinely given a list of precautions they should take, she said, from walking on the lighted side of the street to avoiding earbuds so they can hear what is happening around them. Instead, she said, the standard should be that everyone is safe regardless of the time of day.

items.title: How this Mississauga woman uses her law background to diversify Canada's golf game
items.summary: Amaya Athill is one of this year’s Top 25 Canadian Immigrant Award recipients. Amaya Athill is a recipient of the 2026 Top 25 Canadian Immigrant Award. Born in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda, she started playing golf at age five when her father introduced her to the sport. Throughout her teens, she played competitively across the Caribbean, “but neither of my parents had gone to university, so we didn’t know how to navigate getting me a full-ride scholarship,” said the Mississauga resident. Ultimately, Athill ended up attending university in London, England, however, the parameters around golf scholarships were quite different, so she studied law and built a successful career as a barrister instead. , where she focused on civil litigation, international law and human rights. “I didn’t play golf for many years,” Athill said. But when the pandemic hit, she picked up a club and suddenly saw the sport through a new lens.
